accuracy.evidence: Melting and boiling points (F −220/−188 °C, Cl −101/−34, Br −7/59, I 114/184) match the RSC periodic table and PubChem values rounded to whole degrees. States and colours (pale yellow gas, yellow-green gas, red-brown liquid with orange vapour, grey-black solid with purple vapour) and the displacement series follow AQA 8462 section 4.1.2.6 and OpenStax Chemistry 2e 18.11. Astatine is described only as predicted. The adult text notes chlorine's slightly higher electron affinity so the 'fluorine grabs hardest' model is not overstated.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets real slips: expecting Group 7 reactivity to rise down the group like Group 1; confusing chlorine with chloride; reading the orange of bromine water in KCl as a reaction; thinking a less reactive halogen can 'swap halfway'; writing Cl + I⁻ instead of diatomic Cl₂ + 2I⁻; predicting Cl⁺ or Cl²⁻ for the ion. Each has a predict option, a mastery distractor or a tagged challenge message.

lab_distinct.evidence: Unique mechanics: drag down a Group 7 tile column while a jar redraws each element's real state and colour, drop one electron into the dashed gap of a 2,8,7 shell diagram, compare shell distance and pull arrows for F to I, and drag halogen bottles onto KCl/KBr/KI tubes to fill a 3 × 3 results grid. No shared mechanic with flag_alk.js or flag_hion.js; the 6-shingle gate passed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the pattern before it is named: the states change from gas to liquid to solid as they move down; astatine is predicted from the trend; the full outer shell appears the moment the electron lands; the outer shell visibly moves further out for iodine; then pouring shows only higher-into-lower pairs change colour, and the grid builds the full displacement series with an ionic equation for every reaction.

predictions.evidence: Six predictions with tempting wrong options the lab then tests: bromine as a gas or solid, astatine as a pale gas, Cl⁺ instead of Cl⁻, iodine as most reactive because it is biggest, 'no change' for chlorine water into KBr, and 'they swap halfway' for iodine into KBr. Each reply quotes the learner's choice and explains why the lab disagrees.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Endless generated challenge with three kinds (will it react, what colour, why is the upper halogen more reactive). Wrong answers get tagged explanations: same-halogen pairs, below-versus-above reactivity, orange versus brown confusion and, for bromine into KI, a note that no chlorine is present. Streak counter and 'Another' keep it going without repeating text.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short with one idea each and pass the ≤6.5 grade check; adult paragraphs pass ≤9.5 and define every term (diatomic, displacement, halide ion, shielding) on first use. Lab messages are one or two sentences and name the specific elements involved rather than generic praise.

no_filler.evidence: No stock phrases or padding. Every sentence carries a fact, a reason or an instruction: data values, the ionic equation, the reason for the trend, or what to drag next. The family tip is a concrete 'steal the sock' game that mirrors displacement, not a vague suggestion.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop: canvas uses tall 1.1 on narrow screens so the 3 × 3 grid rows stay legible; bottles are 62 px wide touch targets; bottle-to-tube pours also work as tap bottle then tap tube, and the electron drag and tile slide have button alternatives ('Move the electron into the gap', Up/Down the group). No horizontal overflow in screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports zero violations in light and dark themes. The canvas has a live aria-label describing the current element, atom or every tube's state and selected bottle; controls are real buttons in a labelled group; colour is never the only cue because each result also says 'reacted' or 'no reaction' in text, and reduced motion is respected through the kit.
